narrative.overview:
**Creative North Star: The Annotated Archive.** gendertagger should feel like a carefully maintained working archive: quiet parchment underfoot, compact records in stable places, and annotations that reveal the current path without competing with the evidence. The incumbent interface is intentionally plain enough for long review sessions, yet warm enough to remain human.

Human editorial clarity governs every decision. Interfaces are dense because reviewers compare evidence, not because the product is an operations dashboard. Structure comes from type, spacing, hairline borders, and tonal layers; colour names state function; motion confirms state rather than performing. Avoid consumer-dashboard gloss—no decorative gradients, giant KPI theatre, or floating-card scenery.
keyCharacteristics: Warm, theme-aware neutral surfaces keep evidence dominant.
Annotation violet marks place and selection; registry teal marks action.
Compact system typography supports sustained bilingual review.
Borders and tonal shifts carry structure; shadows belong to overlays.
Canonical vocabulary remains legible in text, not color alone.

rules.name: Annotation Marks Place
rules.body: Annotation Ink is the violet navigation and selection color. It identifies the current route, selected option, or editorial focus. It is not the default call-to-action color.

rules.name: Registry Teal Commits Work
rules.body: Registry Teal belongs to primary actions and deliberate state changes. A view should expose one visually dominant action. Do not spread teal across decoration, charts, or passive metadata.

rules.name: Vocabulary Is Data
rules.body: Male blue, female coral, institution green, and unknown amber are fixed semantic families. Each family has a border, readable text tone, and quiet tint; use all three together. Always print the canonical token or an explicit state alongside color. Certainty tiers reuse these families deliberately: `contested` uses coral, `low` uses amber, and `thin` uses blue.

rules.name: Compact Does Not Mean Cryptic
rules.body: Small text supports comparison only when line height, hierarchy, and plain-language labels remain intact. Do not shrink body copy below the body token to fit more controls.

rules.name: One Main Title
rules.body: Every view has one `page` heading. Panel titles step down to `title`; labels and metadata step down again. Weight establishes hierarchy before size does, so reserve bold weight for display moments and use semibold for operational emphasis.

rules.name: Four-Pixel Cadence
rules.body: Space follows the 4px-based scale. Dense rows use one or two steps internally; cards and panels usually use four; major regions use six to twelve. Prefer `gap` between siblings over compensating margins, and do not introduce off-scale spacing for isolated alignment fixes.

rules.name: Tonal Layers First
rules.body: The page, panel, and raised-surface tones establish hierarchy. Content cards, review rows, inputs, and structural panels stay flat and use hairline borders; they do not cast shadows or lift on hover.

rules.name: Shape Follows Scope
rules.body: The larger the container and interaction scope, the larger its allowed radius. Do not put pill-shaped buttons beside squared operational controls, and do not round every nested surface independently.

rules.name: One Primary Action
rules.body: Component variants describe consequence, not visual preference. Adding another solid button to solve hierarchy confusion is a content-structure failure; clarify the workflow instead.

dos: Do keep evidence, provenance, revision, and uncertainty visible where decisions happen.
Do use semantic tokens so light and dark themes preserve the same hierarchy.
Do retain visible labels, keyboard focus, explicit status text, and bilingual expansion space.
Do use monospace selectively for canonical tokens and machine-stable identifiers.
Do place one primary action per view and keep irreversible actions visibly critical.
Do use borders, alignment, and tonal layers before adding elevation.
donts: Don't introduce consumer-dashboard gloss: gradients, giant KPI theatre, glass effects, or decorative floating cards.
Don't use raw color values in components or repurpose vocabulary colors for unrelated decoration.
Don't communicate selection, certainty, error, or vocabulary through color alone.
Don't translate canonical label and tier tokens or collapse unknown, abstain, missing, and error states.
Don't use generic confidence bars or imply comparability between method scores without evidence.
Don't add shadows to content cards, hover lift to rows, or animation that competes with review work.
Don't invent data, provenance, or interface states to fill an otherwise quiet surface.
